questions.question: A tangent is drawn from an external point P to a circle at point T, and the radius OT is drawn to the point of tangency. What is the measure of angle OTP?
questions.explanation: A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. OT is that radius and TP lies along the tangent, so angle OTP = 90° for every circle and every external point P.
questions.trap: Choices A and C come from assuming the triangle OTP is a 30-60-90 figure and reading off the wrong vertex; B from assuming OTP is isosceles with a 45° base angle. Choice E treats O, T and P as collinear, which would make the 'tangent' pass through the center - a secant, not a tangent. The tangent-radius angle does not depend on the radius or on how far P sits from the center.

questions.question: Chord AB has a length of 10. The center of the circle is O, and the perpendicular from O meets AB at point M. What is the length of AM?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the center of a circle to a chord bisects that chord. So M is the midpoint of AB and AM = AB/2 = 10/2 = 5. The radius is not needed.
questions.trap: Choice A halves the chord twice (10/4), as if the perpendicular cut each half again. Choice D reports the whole chord instead of the half. Choice E multiplies by 2 where the bisection calls for dividing by 2. Choice C splits the chord in a 3:1 ratio, which no circle theorem supports.

questions.question: A circle has radius 13. A chord is drawn such that the perpendicular distance from the center to the chord is 5. What is the length of the chord?

questions.trap: Students forget to double x at the end, giving 12 instead of 24. The perpendicular bisects the chord, so x is only half the chord.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about a tangent to a circle are always true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The tangent meets the circle at exactly one point.
B. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.
C. Two tangents from the same external point have equal length.
D. The tangent passes through the center of the circle.
E. The tangent is parallel to all chords of the circle.
questions.explanation: A: True by definition — a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point. B: True — tangent ⊥ radius is a fundamental theorem. C: True — two tangents from the same external point are always equal. D: False — a line through the center is a secant (or diameter), not a tangent. E: False — a tangent has a specific direction and is not parallel to all chords.
questions.trap: Students often forget option C (equal tangents from an external point) or incorrectly mark D as true, confusing a tangent with a line through the center.
questions.ets_note: Definition checklist, not an ETS-style item.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Textbook definition recall; distractors D and E are throwaway.

questions.question: From external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle. If PO = 17 (O is the center) and the radius = 8, what is the length of each tangent segment PA?
questions.explanation: Since OA ⊥ PA (radius to tangent), triangle OAP is a right triangle with hypotenuse PO = 17 and leg OA = 8. By the Pythagorean theorem: PA² = PO² - OA² = 17² - 8² = 289 - 64 = 225. PA = 15.
questions.trap: Students may add instead of subtract: √(17² + 8²) = √353 ≈ 18.8. Remember OA ⊥ PA, so PO is the hypotenuse and PA is a leg.

questions.question: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc of 80°. What is the measure of the inscribed angle?
questions.explanation: The inscribed angle theorem states that an inscribed angle equals half the central angle that intercepts the same arc. Equivalently, an inscribed angle = ½ × (intercepted arc). Inscribed angle = 80°/2 = 40°.
questions.trap: Students confuse the inscribed angle with the central angle: they set inscribed angle = intercepted arc = 80° instead of dividing by 2.
questions.ets_note: Direct theorem recall.

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD intersect inside a circle at point P. If AP = 4, PB = 9, and CP = 6, what is PD?
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem (Power of a Point for two chords): AP × PB = CP × PD. Substituting: 4 × 9 = 6 × PD. 36 = 6 × PD. PD = 6.
questions.trap: Students multiply the full chord by the full chord: (AP + PB)(CP + PD) = 13 × (6 + PD), which is wrong. The theorem uses each chord's two segments separately: AP × PB = CP × PD.

questions.question: A circle has center O and radius 5. Chord AB is 6 units long. What is the distance from the center O to chord AB?

questions.question: A circle with center O has radius 7. Point P is outside the circle, with PO = 25. Segments PA and PB are tangent to the circle at A and B. What is the area of quadrilateral OAPB?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Find PA using the right triangle OAP (right angle at A, since radius ⊥ tangent). PA² = PO² - OA² = 25² - 7² = 625 - 49 = 576. PA = 24. Step 2: By the equal-tangents theorem, PB = PA = 24. Step 3: Quadrilateral OAPB is made of two congruent right triangles OAP and OBP. Area of triangle OAP = (1/2) × OA × PA = (1/2) × 7 × 24 = 84. Total area of OAPB = 2 × 84 = 168.
questions.trap: Students may compute area = PO × OA = 25 × 7 = 175 (incorrectly treating OAPB as a rectangle with sides PO and OA). The figure is a kite, not a rectangle, and the area uses the right-angle legs OA and PA.

questions.question: A chord PQ of a circle passes through the center of the circle. Which of the following are necessarily true? Select all that apply.
options: A. PQ is a diameter of the circle.
B. PQ is the longest chord of the circle.
C. The distance from the center to PQ is positive.
D. PQ subtends a semicircle on each side.
E. Any inscribed angle that intercepts PQ as its arc measures 90°.
questions.explanation: A: True — a chord through the center is by definition a diameter. B: True — the diameter is the longest chord. C: False — the center lies on PQ, so its distance from PQ is 0. D: True — a diameter divides the circle into two equal semicircles. E: True — by Thales' theorem, any inscribed angle intercepting a semicircle (180° arc) = 90°.
questions.trap: Students often omit E, forgetting that any angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. Some also pick C, assuming every chord is some positive distance from the center, when a chord through the center is at distance 0.
questions.ets_note: Option E wording 'intercepts PQ as its arc' is clumsy; definition checklist.

questions.question:
Circle has radius 5. Chord A is at distance 3 from the center. Chord B is at distance 4 from the center.
Quantity A: Length of Chord A
Quantity B: Length of Chord B
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: For Chord A (distance 3): half-chord = √(5² - 3²) = √(25-9) = √16 = 4. Chord A = 8. For Chord B (distance 4): half-chord = √(5² - 4²) = √(25-16) = √9 = 3. Chord B = 6. Quantity A (8) > Quantity B (6).
questions.trap: Students may reason that a greater distance from the center means a longer chord (backwards). In fact, chords closer to the center are longer — the chord at distance 3 is longer than the chord at distance 4.

questions.question: From external point P, a tangent PT touches a circle at T, and a secant through P meets the circle at A and B (PA < PB). If PT = 6 and the chord AB = 5, what is PA?
questions.explanation: Let PA = x. Then PB = PA + AB = x + 5. Power of a Point (tangent-secant): PT² = PA × PB. 36 = x(x + 5). x² + 5x - 36 = 0. Factor: (x + 9)(x - 4) = 0. x = 4 (rejecting x = -9 since length is positive). PA = 4.
questions.trap: Students may try PT = (PA + PB)/2 or PT² = PA × AB = 6 × 5 = 30, confusing AB (the chord) with PB (the full secant distance). They should set PB = PA + AB and solve the resulting quadratic.

questions.question: In a circle with center O and radius 10, chord AB and chord CD intersect at P inside the circle. AP = 2, and PB = 8 times AP. CP = CD/3. What is the length of chord CD?
questions.explanation: Step 1: AP = 2, PB = 8 × 2 = 16. Step 2: By the intersecting chords theorem: AP × PB = CP × PD. So 2 × 16 = 32. Step 3: Let CD = L. Since CP = CD/3 = L/3, it follows that PD = CD - CP = L - L/3 = 2L/3. Step 4: CP × PD = (L/3)(2L/3) = 2L²/9 = 32. So L² = 32 × 9/2 = 144. L = 12. CD = 12.
questions.trap: Students may incorrectly assume PD = CD/3 as well (treating P as the midpoint), writing CP × PD = (L/3)² = 32, giving L = √288 ≈ 17. The point P is NOT necessarily the midpoint; CP = L/3 forces PD = 2L/3.

questions.question: A circle has center O and radius r. From external point P, two tangents PA and PB are drawn (PA = PB = 15). The angle APB = 60°. What is the radius r?
questions.explanation:
Tangent segments from P are equal, and OP bisects angle APB, so angle APO = 30°. A radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent, so angle OAP = 90°. Triangle OAP is therefore a 30-60-90 triangle with the 30° angle at P.
PA = 15 is opposite the 60° angle at O, so it is the long leg. The short leg OA = r is opposite the 30° angle, so 15 = r√3 and r = 15/√3 = 5√3.
questions.trap: Students who find the altitude of the equilateral triangle APB, 15√3/2, instead of the radius choose D; those who think r = AB = 15 choose E.

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD intersect at point P inside a circle. AP = 3, PB = 12, CP = 4. Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.
options: B. Chord AB is longer than chord CD.
C. The product AP × PB equals the product CP × PD.
D. Chord AB and chord CD have the same length.
questions.explanation: By intersecting chords: AP × PB = CP × PD. 3 × 12 = 4 × PD. PD = 9. A: True. C: True (this is the theorem). B: AB = AP + PB = 3 + 12 = 15. CD = CP + PD = 4 + 9 = 13. AB (15) > CD (13). B is true. D: 15 ≠ 13, so false. E: PD = (AP × PB)/CP = (3 × 12)/4 = 9. But option E says PD = CP × PB / AP = 4 × 12 / 3 = 16 ≠ 9. E is false.
questions.trap: Students may believe D is true, assuming intersecting chords are always equal. They are not — the theorem constrains the products of segments, not the chord lengths themselves.

questions.question: From external point P, a secant intersects a circle at A and B with AB = 8 (A is closer to P). A tangent from P to the circle has length PT = x + 2, and PA = x. What is the value of PB?
questions.explanation: Step 1: PB = PA + AB = x + 8. Step 2: Tangent-secant Power of a Point: PT² = PA × PB. Substituting: (x + 2)² = x(x + 8). Step 3: Expand: x² + 4x + 4 = x² + 8x. Step 4: Simplify: 4x + 4 = 8x → 4 = 4x → x = 1. Step 5: PA = 1, PB = 1 + 8 = 9. Verify: PT = x + 2 = 3. PT² = 9 = PA × PB = 1 × 9 = 9. ✓ PB = 9.
questions.trap: Students set PT² = PA × AB = 3² = 9 = 1 × 8 (using the chord length AB instead of PB). The tangent-secant formula requires PT² = PA × PB where PB is the distance from P to the far intersection, not the chord length.

questions.question: From external point P, a tangent PT touches a circle (center O, radius 5) at T, with OP = 13. A second tangent from P touches the circle at S. Chord TS is drawn. What is the length of chord TS?
questions.explanation: Step 1: PT² = OP² - r² = 169 - 25 = 144. PT = 12. By equal tangents, PS = 12 also. Step 2: The chord TS connects the two points of tangency. In kite OTPS (where OT ⊥ PT and OS ⊥ PS), the diagonals OP and TS are perpendicular and OP bisects TS. Step 3: Using coordinates — place O at origin, P at (13, 0). By symmetry, T and S are symmetric about the x-axis. T = (r²/OP, r·PT/OP) = (25/13, 60/13). By symmetry S = (25/13, -60/13). Step 4: TS = distance from T to S = |60/13 - (-60/13)| = 120/13.
questions.trap: Students may compute TS = 2 × OT = 10 (doubling the radius, confusing TS with the diameter), or use TS = PT = 12 (confusing the tangent length with the chord). The chord TS requires the symmetric coordinate geometry approach.

questions.question: In a circle, chord PQ is perpendicular to diameter AB at point M. AM = 4 and MB = 9. What is the length of PM (half the chord PQ)?
questions.explanation: When a chord is perpendicular to the diameter and meets it at M, the intersecting chords theorem applies: PM × MQ = AM × MB. Since PM = MQ (the diameter bisects a perpendicular chord), PM² = AM × MB = 4 × 9 = 36. PM = 6.
questions.trap: Students may use the Pythagorean theorem with the radius: radius = (4+9)/2 = 6.5, then PM² = 6.5² - 2.5² = 42.25 - 6.25 = 36, PM = 6. This gives the same answer, but the elegant method is the intersecting chords theorem: PM² = AM × MB.

questions.question: A circle with center O has radius 10. Two parallel chords AB and CD are on opposite sides of the center. AB = 16 and CD = 12. What is the distance between the two chords?
questions.explanation: Distance from center to chord AB: half of AB = 8. d₁² + 8² = 10². d₁² = 100 - 64 = 36. d₁ = 6. Distance from center to chord CD: half of CD = 6. d₂² + 6² = 10². d₂² = 100 - 36 = 64. d₂ = 8. Since the chords are on opposite sides of the center, total distance = d₁ + d₂ = 6 + 8 = 14.

questions.question: In a circle of radius 10, two chords AB and CD intersect at point P. AB = 12, with AP = 3 and PB = 9. If CP = 3 × PD, what is the length of chord CD?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Apply the intersecting chords theorem: AP × PB = CP × PD. So 3 × 9 = 27 = CP × PD. Step 2: Let PD = x. Then CP = 3x (given CP = 3 × PD). Substituting: 3x × x = 3x² = 27. x² = 9. x = 3. PD = 3, CP = 9. Step 3: CD = CP + PD = 9 + 3 = 12.
questions.trap: Students may compute CD = CP = 3 × PD and then mistakenly use CD as if it equals CP alone (reporting 9), forgetting to add PD to get the full chord. Also, some students set AP × PB = AP + PB = 12 (adding instead of multiplying), giving wrong products.

questions.question: Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at point P. AP = 5, PB = 9, CP = x and PD = x + 4. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Apply the intersecting chords theorem: AP × PB = CP × PD. So 5 × 9 = 45 = x(x + 4). Step 2: Expand: x² + 4x - 45 = 0. Step 3: Factor: (x + 9)(x - 5) = 0. Step 4: x = 5 (rejecting x = -9 since a length must be positive). Verify: CP = 5, PD = 9, CP × PD = 45 = AP × PB ✓.
questions.trap: Students may set CP × PD = AP + PB = 14 (adding instead of multiplying), giving x(x+4) = 14 → x² + 4x - 14 = 0, which has an irrational solution. The intersecting chords theorem requires multiplication: AP × PB.

questions.question:
Circle O has radius 5. Point P is outside the circle with PO = 13. A line through P meets the circle at two points, C and D, with C nearer to P.

Which of the following values are possible for PC?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation:
The tangent from P has length √(13² - 5²) = √144 = 12. For any line through P that meets the circle at C and D, PC × PD equals the square of this tangent length, so PC × PD = 144.
PC is smallest when the line passes through O: PC = 13 - 5 = 8. As the line tilts toward a tangent, PC increases toward 12 but never reaches it, because at PC = 12 the two points coincide. So 8 <= PC < 12.
A (6): less than 8. Not possible.
B (8): PD = 144/8 = 18, a valid chord of length 10 through O. Possible.
C (9): PD = 144/9 = 16, so CD = 7. Possible.
D (12): PD = 12, so C and D coincide (tangent). Not possible.
E (16): PD = 144/16 = 9 < PC, contradicting C being nearer. Not possible.
The answers are B and C.
questions.trap: Students who accept any value of PC from 8 up (taking D, PC = 12, because 12 is the tangent length) forget that a tangent touches the circle only once; others pick E because 16 < 18 = 13 + 5.

changes: explanation rewritten: removed mid-text self-corrections, states the range 8 <= PC < 12 explicitly
stem: dropped redundant 'Select all that apply' and described the line directly
note: relies on the secant-tangent relation, which sits at the edge of the ETS syllabus

questions.question: In a circle, chords PQ and RS are perpendicular and intersect at point T. PT = 4, TQ = 9, and RT = 6. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords relationship, PT × TQ = RT × TS, so 36 = 6 × TS and TS = 6. Place T at the origin with P = (−4, 0), Q = (9, 0), R = (0, 6), S = (0, −6). The center lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ, x = 2.5, and on the perpendicular bisector of RS, y = 0. So the center is (2.5, 0) and the radius is the distance to P: 2.5 + 4 = 6.5.
questions.trap: Students treat half of a chord as the radius, e.g. 12/2 = 6, or find TS = 6 and stop, or compute √(4²+6²) without locating the center.

Quantity A: the radius of the circle
Quantity B: (p + q)/2

questions.explanation: Slide each of the two perpendicular segments sideways until it lies on the line through O that is perpendicular to CD. Sliding EF toward that line can only lengthen the part of it that reaches the circle, and the same is true for GH, because the longest chord perpendicular to CD is the one through the center. Stacked end to end on that central line, the two lengths would together fill at most a full diameter, so p + q is at most 2r. Since neither segment actually passes through O, at least one of the two slides strictly lengthens, so p + q is less than 2r and (p + q)/2 is less than r. Quantity A is greater.

The comparison is with half of that total, not the total itself, and the ceiling on p + q is the diameter — a ceiling that can only be reached by a segment running straight through the center, which this figure rules out.

questions.explanation: Two sides of triangle AOB are radii, so OA = OB = k and the perimeter is 2k + AB. questions.question:
O is a point in a plane, and X, Y and Z are three distinct points in that same plane with OX = OY = OZ = 9.
Quantity A: XY
Quantity B: YZ
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Saying that X, Y and Z are all 9 units from O places all three on one circle of radius 9 centered at O, but it says nothing about where on that circle they sit. The length XY depends only on the central angle XOY, and YZ only on the central angle YOZ, and those two angles are completely free. For instance, putting X, Y and Z at 0, 60 and 180 degrees around the circle makes XY = 9 and YZ = 9*sqrt(3), so Quantity B wins; swapping the roles of X and Z makes Quantity A win. Nothing decides between them.
questions.trap: Students read three equal distances from one point as forcing an equilateral triangle and answer 'equal'. Equal distances from O only put the three points on a common circle; the chords between them still vary with how the points are spaced around it.
questions.ets_note: Two quick cases settle it; labelled hard but is easy to medium.

questions.question: In the figure, lines PS and PT touch the circle with center O at S and T. Point R lies on the shorter arc ST. Angle PSR measures 24 degrees and angle PTR measures 31 degrees. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle SPT?
questions.explanation:
An angle between a tangent and a chord equals half the arc it cuts off.
Angle PSR = 24 degrees, so arc SR = 48 degrees. Angle PTR = 31 degrees, so arc RT = 62 degrees.
The shorter arc ST = 48 + 62 = 110 degrees, so the central angle SOT = 110 degrees.
Radii OS and OT are perpendicular to the tangents, so in quadrilateral PSOT: angle SPT = 360 - 90 - 90 - 110 = 70 degrees.
Check with the tangent-tangent rule: angle SPT = 180 - (shorter arc) = 180 - 110 = 70.
questions.trap: Adding the two tangent-chord angles, 24 + 31 = 55, without doubling them to arcs (option A); or giving the angle SRT = 180 - 55 = 125 (option D).

questions.question: A classroom model shows a planet as a circle of radius 5 cm and a satellite's orbit as a concentric circle of radius 5*sqrt(2) cm. At the satellite's position S on the orbit, the two tangent lines from S touch the planet at points A and B, and the planet's surface points on the shorter arc AB are 'in range' of the satellite. Treat the planet as stationary. The satellite takes exactly 3 hours for one full trip around its orbit and moves at constant speed. During one trip, for how many minutes is a fixed point on the planet's surface in range of the satellite?
questions.explanation:
Tangent radius OA is perpendicular to SA, so triangle OAS has a right angle at A, with OA = 5 and hypotenuse OS = 5*sqrt(2).
By the Pythagorean theorem, SA = sqrt(50 - 25) = 5 = OA, so triangle OAS is an isosceles right (45-45-90) triangle and angle AOS = 45 degrees. By symmetry angle BOS = 45 degrees, so angle AOB = 90 degrees.
A fixed point F on the planet's surface is in range exactly when angle FOS is at most 45 degrees (at exactly 45 degrees, S lies on the tangent line at F). So S must be within 45 degrees on either side of ray OF: a 90-degree stretch of its orbit.
Fraction of the trip = 90/360 = 1/4, and the trip lasts 180 minutes, so the time is 180/4 = 45 minutes.
questions.trap: Using only angle AOS = 45 degrees (half of the arc) as the central angle gives 1/8 of the trip, 22.5 minutes (choice A).
